_comment: The eval's own workload and grader: darkmux processes this eval, this folder defines it. `darkmux lab fixture register <this repo>`, then `darkmux lab run salt-shaker -p <profile>`. Implement-from-ticket: the suite check runs the result's own tests plus the hidden AUTH-77 checks in eval/hidden/, which eval/build_workload.py embeds into the suite command (the grader runs that command in a copy of the result, where eval/ does not exist). The report reads 'N passing, M failing' over all of them. Scope is not graded: the ticket requires source changes, and darkmux's scope check cannot allow edits to existing files. timingSafeEqual is in the ticket but not graded: no behavioral test can observe it. The sandbox and the grader run in the pinned Node 24 image (workload.image; Node runs the .ts files directly), not darkmux's default image. This folder is never copied into the model's sandbox.

workload.description: Implement-from-ticket on the public salt-shaker fixture (github.com/kstrat2001/salt-shaker, MIT): move an account service from unsalted SHA-256 to salted scrypt, upgrading existing users on sign-in. Graded by hidden tests, one per ticket requirement.
workload.prompt:
TICKET AUTH-77 — Store passwords with salted scrypt ## Background The account service stores every password as unsalted SHA-256. One leaked database would let anyone with a GPU recover most passwords within days, and identical passwords show up as identical hashes. This ticket moves new and changed passwords to salted scrypt and upgrades existing users as they sign in. The code lives at: - ${SANDBOX_DIR}/src/passwords.ts (hashing and verification) - ${SANDBOX_DIR}/src/accounts.ts (sign-up, sign-in, password changes) Existing tests: - ${SANDBOX_DIR}/test/accounts.test.ts - ${SANDBOX_DIR}/test/portability.test.ts (a guard on the suite itself; leave it alone) ## Requirements 1. `hashPassword(password)` in `src/passwords.ts` returns `scrypt$$$

$$`: N = 16384, r = 8, p = 1, `` is 16 random bytes generated fresh for every call, `` is the 64-byte scrypt key, both base64. Hashing the same password twice gives two different strings. 2. `verifyPassword(password, stored)` returns `true` when the password matches a `scrypt$` string and `false` otherwise. It never throws: a malformed or unknown stored value returns `false`. Compare the keys with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. 3. `verifyPassword` reads N, r and p from the stored string, so a hash made with other parameters still verifies. 4. Passwords are normalized to Unicode NFC before hashing and before verifying, so the same password typed as composed or decomposed characters is accepted. 5. Export `WeakPassword` (an `Error` subclass) from `src/accounts.ts`. `register` and `changePassword` throw it when the new password is shorter than 12 or longer than 256 characters, counted after normalization. Nothing is stored when they throw. 6. Export `InvalidCredentials` (an `Error` subclass) from `src/accounts.ts`. `login` throws it, with the same message, for an unknown email and for a wrong password, so a caller cannot tell which accounts exist. `changePassword` with a wrong current password throws it too, and changes nothing. 7. Existing users keep their `sha256$` hashes until they sign in. A successful `login` with a `sha256$` hash replaces it with a fresh `scrypt$` hash of the same password. A failed `login` leaves the stored hash untouched. 8. A successful `login` with a `scrypt$` hash whose N is below 16384 also replaces it with a fresh hash at the current parameters. 9. The stored record never contains the plaintext password, in any field. ## Constraints - Repo root: ${SANDBOX_DIR}. - Use only Node's standard library (`node:crypto` has `scryptSync`, `randomBytes` and `timingSafeEqual`). There is no install step. - This is TypeScript that Node runs directly, with no build step: Node strips the types. Use only syntax that can be stripped (no `enum`, `namespace` or constructor parameter properties) and import local files with their `.ts` extension. There is no type checker in this environment. - Add your tests for the new behavior in a new file under `test/`. Do not change the existing test files at all. Tests must not embed absolute paths. - Iterate by running the suite: cd ${SANDBOX_DIR} && npm test - Final verification is the same command: cd ${SANDBOX_DIR} && npm test ## When you're done You're done when every requirement above is implemented and covered by a test, and `npm test` is green. ## Reply format Keep it tight: - What you changed: files and a one-line summary each - Requirements: one line per numbered requirement, saying where it is handled - Tests: how many you added, and the `# pass N` line from your final run - Anything in the ticket you found ambiguous, and how you read it

asks: Final verification is the same command:
Do not change the existing test files at all.
Tests must not embed absolute paths.

criteria.name: Salted scrypt hash
criteria.description: hashPassword returns scrypt$N$r$p$salt$hash at N=16384, r=8, p=1, with a fresh 16-byte salt every call.

source.anchor: it("r1 hash has the scrypt format and parameters"

tests: r1 hash has the scrypt format and parameters
r1 hash key is the scrypt key of the password and salt
r1 hashing the same password twice gives different salts

criteria.name: Verify never throws
criteria.description: verifyPassword accepts the right password, refuses a wrong one, and returns false for a malformed stored value instead of throwing.

source.anchor: it("r2 verify accepts the right password and refuses a wrong one"

tests: r2 verify accepts the right password and refuses a wrong one
r2 verify returns false for malformed stored values without throwing

criteria.name: Parameters read from the hash
criteria.description: verifyPassword reads N, r and p from the stored string, so a hash made with other parameters still verifies.

tests: r3 verify reads N, r and p from the stored string

criteria.description: Composed and decomposed forms of the same password both verify.
